paper.citation: Gardiner C, Weakley J, Burke LM, Roach GD, Sargent C, Maniar N, Huynh M, Miller DJ, Townshend A, Halson SL. The effect of alcohol on subsequent sleep in healthy adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sleep Medicine Reviews. 2025;80:102030.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis pooled 27 controlled experimental studies of healthy adults aged 18 to 70 who received an acute alcohol dose before a night-time sleep opportunity, mostly within 3 h of bedtime. Low doses (up to 0.50 g/kg) reduced REM sleep and delayed REM sleep onset, with effects becoming larger at higher doses. High doses (at least 0.85 g/kg) shortened sleep onset latency and latency to N3 sleep, while effects on total sleep time, sleep efficiency and wake after sleep onset were uncertain.
paper.tldr: In healthy adults, a low dose of alcohol taken before bed delays and reduces REM sleep, with larger doses causing more disruption; only high doses shorten sleep onset, and that benefit comes with further REM loss.
paper.methods: Systematic searches of PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science followed PRISMA 2020, with two reviewers screening and coding studies. Risk of bias was assessed with the RoB 2 crossover tool, and effects were pooled with multilevel mixed-effects meta-analysis and dose meta-regression.
paper.findings: A low dose (about 0.35 to 0.50 g/kg) was associated with a longer REM sleep onset latency (+18.0 min, 95% CI 8.8 to 27.1; k=29) and reduced REM sleep duration (-11.3 min, 95% CI -20.8 to -1.8; k=13), and larger doses produced greater REM reductions. Sleep onset latency was shortened only at a high dose (about 0.85 g/kg), and latency to N3 sleep was shortened at about 0.95 g/kg. Pooled effects on total sleep time (-10.1 min, 95% CI -24.6 to 4.4), sleep efficiency and wake after sleep onset were not significant, with wide prediction intervals, and the review could not determine a sex effect.
paper.limitations: Most included studies (21 of 27) had a risk of bias concern, and many had small samples. Alcohol was given mostly within 3 h of bedtime, so the effect of timing could not be determined, and beverage types varied. Results apply to healthy adults aged 18 to 70, not to athletes, adolescents or people with sleep disorders, and dose thresholds rest on statistical significance.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff advising athletes on evening alcohol should know that a low dose taken within a few hours of bedtime can reduce REM sleep, and that larger doses cause more disruption. The review concludes that alcohol is not an appropriate sleep aid, because the REM disruption outweighs the faster sleep onset seen at high doses. The effect of timing and of sex remains unclear.
paper.athleteDev: Use these dose-related findings in education on evening alcohol intake and sleep quality for athletes. The review did not measure athletic performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The review did not study injured athletes or return-to-sport decisions. It should not be used to set return-to-sport timing or clearance, or to give alcohol guidance after injury.
